question: Inhibin: a new circulating marker of hydatidiform mole?
answer: Serum inhibin is elevated in patients with newly diagnosed complete hydatidiform mole (median 8.3 U/ml vs 2.8 U/ml in normal pregnancy at the same stage), and molar tissue contains high inhibin concentrations, supporting it as a circulating marker. Serum inhibin fell significantly 7 to 10 days after mole evacuation to levels similar to the normal follicular phase, whereas hCG remained far above non-pregnant levels. None of the four patients with post-evacuation inhibin of 0.4 U/ml or less developed persistent trophoblastic disease. In a study of 17 patients with molar or choriocarcinoma placental tumours, inhibin A was increased in 10/17 and inhibin B in 4/17 patients. Inhibin A correlated with hCG during chemotherapy follow-up, and normalized faster than hCG or hCGbeta in some patients.

question: Discharging patients earlier from Winnipeg hospitals: does it adversely affect quality of care?
answer: In Winnipeg's seven large acute care hospitals, length of stay fell significantly (11.1% to 22.0%) over 1989-90 to 1992-93 across four diagnostic categories, without a consistent rise in 30-day readmission rates for AMI, bronchitis/asthma or TURP, so earlier discharge did not appear to adversely affect quality of care. Readmission rate for uterine or adnexal procedures rose significantly between the first and second year (p=0.04) but then stayed constant over the next three years. Mean physician visits within 30 days after discharge changed little (a slight rise for AMI in year one, a slight decrease for bronchitis/asthma), and no correlation was found between hospital length of stay and readmission rates or physician visits in 1992-93.

Readmission rate for uterine or adnexal procedures rose significantly between the first and second year (p=0.04) but then stayed constant over the next three years.

Mean physician visits within 30 days after discharge changed little (a slight rise for AMI in year one, a slight decrease for bronchitis/asthma), and no correlation was found between hospital length of stay and readmission rates or physician visits in 1992-93.

limitations.text: The Winnipeg study was a retrospective descriptive study that used only readmission and physician visits within 30 days as proxies for quality, so it cannot establish causation and does not capture other aspects of quality such as mortality or patient experience.

question: Are head and neck specific quality of life measures necessary?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 55 head and neck cancer patients, the Head & Neck Survey correlated more strongly with other head and neck-specific measures than with a general health measure, indicating that head and neck-specific health status domains are distinct from those assessed by general QOL measures. Eating/swallowing and speech/communication domains were not well correlated with general health domains, and appearance was not fully reflected by any other domain, suggesting general measures do not fully capture these aspects. Head and neck pain was highly correlated with general bodily pain (r=0.88, p<.0001), so this domain overlaps substantially with a general measure.

question: Does the SCL 90-R obsessive-compulsive dimension identify cognitive impairments?
answer: In 19 adults with malignant brain tumors, the SCL 90-R Obsessive-Compulsive subscale was not related to objective measures of attention, verbal memory, or age, so it did not identify objectively measured cognitive impairment. question: Hypotension in patients with coronary disease: can profound hypotensive events cause myocardial ischaemic events?
answer: In patients with ischaemic heart disease on hypotensive drugs, ST-segment ischaemic events were significantly associated with preceding hypotensive events (chi2 = 40.2, p<0.0001), and 14 hypotension-induced ischaemic events occurred in 8 of 25 patients. question: Fatigue in primary Sjögren's syndrome: is there a link with the fibromyalgia syndrome?
answer: In this study, fibromyalgia (FM) could account for only a small share of fatigue in primary Sjögren's syndrome (pSS). Fatigue was reported by 50 of 74 pSS patients (68%), while FM was present in only 9 of 74 (12%), so at most 9 of the 50 fatigued patients could have had FM. Fatigue was significantly more common in pSS (68%) than in lupus patients (108/216, 50%; p<0.0087). FM was numerically more frequent in pSS (12%) than in lupus (5%), and was absent in the 13 lupus patients with secondary Sjögren's syndrome. The authors noted that these figures did not match previously reported FM rates in pSS.

question: Is alexithymia a risk factor for unexplained physical symptoms in general medical outpatients?
answer: In a cross-sectional study of 321 internal medicine outpatients, those with medically unexplained physical symptoms (169 patients) were overall not more alexithymic than patients with explained symptoms, so alexithymia was not shown to be a risk factor. Among patients with unexplained symptoms, alexithymia was not associated with subjective health experience or use of medical services. Higher alexithymia was found only in a subgroup: patients with both unexplained symptoms and a mental disorder who denied any connection between emotional problems and their physical symptoms.

answer: In 30 patients with critical leg ischemia and insufficient venous material, semiclosed SFA endarterectomy combined with a short venous bypass gave cumulative primary patency of 60.3% at 1 year and 48.4% at 3 years, with limb salvage of 68.6% at both 1 and 3 years.

question: Antral follicle assessment as a tool for predicting outcome in IVF--is it a better predictor than age and FSH?
answer: In a prospective study of 224 IVF patients, baseline antral follicle count >6 was associated with a markedly higher clinical pregnancy rate than count ≤6 (51% vs 19%), and this difference remained significant after controlling for maternal age and basal FSH. Cycle cancellation was far more frequent with antral follicle count ≤6 than >6 (33% vs 1%); cancellation also rose with advancing age and elevated basal FSH, but antral follicle assessment added independent information beyond them. In a separate cohort of IVF/ICSI pregnancies, AFC was the only ovarian reserve marker (compared with FSH, basal oestradiol and oestradiol response) that differed between miscarriage and ongoing pregnancy groups, though its discriminative ability for miscarriage was low (AUC 0.588).

question: Acute respiratory distress syndrome in children with malignancy--can we predict outcome?
answer: In a retrospective review of 17 children with malignancy and ARDS on mechanical ventilation, peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP and ventilation index values distinguished survivors from non-survivors by day 3, so outcome could be predicted from early respiratory data. Oxygenation efficiency measures (PaO2/FIO2 and P(A-a)O2) were significantly related to outcome only from day 8 after the start of mechanical ventilation, so they were later predictors. Only 6 of 17 children (35.3%) survived, and sepsis syndrome was present in 70.6% of the children.

question: Does tranexamic acid reduce desmopressin-induced hyperfibrinolysis?
answer: In a randomized trial of 100 CABG patients, adding tranexamic acid to desmopressin reduced fibrinolysis and bleeding compared with desmopressin alone: fibrin split products were lower (13.5 vs 21.2 ng/mL) and fibrinogen was higher (167 vs 113 mg/dL). The tranexamic acid plus desmopressin group had less postoperative drainage (623 vs 1010 mL), fewer red cell units (0.9 vs 2.1) and fresh frozen plasma units (0.76 vs 1.84) transfused, and fewer patients needing donor blood products (24% vs 74%). Postoperative hemoglobin was higher with combined tranexamic acid and desmopressin than with desmopressin alone (9.1 vs 7.6 g/dL).

question: Is specialty care associated with improved survival of patients with congestive heart failure?
answer: In a retrospective cohort of 11,661 VA patients discharged with CHF, patients receiving both general medicine and cardiology (mixed) outpatient care had the best 1-year survival (unadjusted mortality 19%), and those receiving general medicine only (RR 1.26) or neither (RR 1.48) had significantly higher adjusted risk of death. Cardiology-only care did not differ significantly from mixed care in adjusted mortality (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.94-1.34), suggesting that the survival benefit is tied to cardiology involvement in addition to or instead of general medicine rather than to general medicine alone. The survival difference between general-medicine-only and mixed care was replicated in a second VHA cohort discharged in 1994-1995 (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.14-1.37).

question: Locoregional opening of the rodent blood-brain barrier for paclitaxel using Nd:YAG laser-induced thermo therapy: a new concept of adjuvant glioma therapy?
answer: In rats, Nd:YAG laser-induced thermotherapy (LITT) of the forebrain opened the blood-brain barrier locally, shown by regional extravasation of Evans blue, C3C, fibrinogen and IgM, and HPLC confirmed that paclitaxel passed across the disrupted barrier into brain tissue. The authors proposed this LITT-induced locoregional BBB disruption as a possible route for passing chemotherapeutic agents into brain tissue to treat malignant glioma.

question: Can progression of valvar aortic stenosis be predicted accurately?
answer: Progression of valvar aortic stenosis was found to be sufficiently predictable for clinical purposes, with the rate depending on the degree of valvar calcification and on the initial transaortic gradient, which relates exponentially to progression. Progression rate was exponentially correlated with initial aortic valve opening area and depended on calcification grade. Calcification-specific area thresholds (AVA below 0.75 cm2 with VC 0, 0.8 with VC I, 0.9 with VC II, 1.0 with VC III) identified valves likely to need surgery in the following years. Age, sex and etiology of the valve obstruction did not significantly influence progression of aortic stenosis in either analysis.

question: Does early discharge with nurse home visits affect adequacy of newborn metabolic screening?
answer: In a single-hospital study, early discharge (24-47 hours) was associated with more initially inadequate newborn metabolic screening specimens (22.9% vs 14.3%), but also with more repeat testing and a higher rate of adequate specimens within the first 9 days of life (98.8% vs 96.7%). question: Sub-classification of low-grade cerebellar astrocytoma: is it clinically meaningful?
answer: In a Danish cohort of children with cerebellar astrocytoma (overall survival 81% at 15-40 years), histological sub-classification was not prognostically meaningful: survival did not differ between pilocytic and fibrillary astrocytoma. The Kernohan and WHO grading systems had no predictive value, and the Daumas-Duport system was unsuitable as a prognostic tool for low-grade posterior fossa astrocytomas. Survival was instead associated with surgically gross-total tumour removal and with tumour location in the cerebellum proper rather than the fourth ventricle.

question: Juvenile ankylosing spondylitis--is it the same disease as adult ankylosing spondylitis?
answer: In a retrospective review of 210 Indian AS patients, juvenile-onset AS (onset before age 17) differed from adult-onset AS in presentation and outcome, suggesting they are not identical in clinical expression. Valvular dysfunction was seen only in patients with juvenile AS in this cohort.

question: Is eligibility for a chemotherapy protocol a good prognostic factor for invasive bladder cancer after radical cystectomy?
answer: In a study of patients undergoing radical cystectomy for invasive bladder cancer, those eligible for and entered into an adjuvant chemotherapy protocol had better outcomes than matched and remaining non-protocol patients, with median overall survival of 76.3 vs 52.1 vs 20.3 months. Median recurrence-free survival was also longer in the protocol group (67.2 months) than in the matched (16.0 months) and remaining (9.4 months) groups. Tumor progression occurred in 46% of the protocol group versus 69% and 65% (P<.05), and cancer-related death in 40% versus 57% and 56%. The advantage was seen even though the protocol's trial result was negative, suggesting that eligibility itself, rather than the chemotherapy, was associated with better prognosis.

question: Are physicians aware of the side effects of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors?

question: Can bedside assessment reliably exclude aspiration following acute stroke?
answer: In a prospective study of 94 acute stroke patients compared against videofluoroscopy, bedside assessment by a speech and language therapist had only 47% sensitivity (NPV 85%), and aspiration was undetected at the bedside in 10 of 20 aspirating patients, so it could not reliably exclude aspiration. The best-performing combination of bedside elements (weak voluntary cough plus any alteration in conscious level) reached 75% sensitivity, 72% specificity and 91% NPV, which is still not enough to rule aspiration out with confidence. Bedside-detected dysphagia in acute stroke was associated with worse outcomes such as chest infection, poor nutrition and death, and in that study videofluoroscopy did not add to the value of bedside assessment for detecting aspiration.

question: Is fetal gender associated with emergency department visits for asthma during pregnancy?
answer: Fetal gender was not associated with having an emergency department visit for asthma during pregnancy (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85-1.19) in a linked administrative database analysis of 109,173 live singleton deliveries, of which 530 women had an asthma ED visit. Among women who had an asthma ED visit during pregnancy, fetal gender was also not a significant predictor of adverse pregnancy outcomes (low birth weight, preterm delivery, Caesarian delivery). ED visits for asthma during pregnancy were instead positively associated with teenage pregnancy, low income, and pregnancy-induced hypertension.

question: Do French lay people and health professionals find it acceptable to breach confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from a sexually transmitted disease?
answer: Acceptability of breaching confidentiality to protect a patient's wife from an STD depended on the group and on the circumstances. Lay people (mean rating 11.76) and psychologists (9.28) rated it as more acceptable than physicians (2.90) on a 0-22 scale. The patient's stated intentions to protect his wife and to inform her of the disease had the greatest impact on whether breaching confidentiality was judged acceptable. Lay participants split into clusters. 14 found breach "always acceptable", 87 said it "depends on the many circumstances", 30 required "consultation with an expert", and 13 found it "never acceptable".

question: Chemotherapy and survival in advanced non-small cell lung carcinoma: is pneumologists' skepticism justified?
answer: In a study of 190 patients with advanced NSCLC (stage IV or IIIB), cytostatic treatment was an independent predictor of survival (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.25-2.76, P=.002), alongside absence of weight loss and ECOG score 0-1, which supports the benefit of chemotherapy in routine care and argues against the skepticism. Even among patients with ECOG 2, survival was somewhat longer with cytostatic treatment than with symptomatic treatment (15 vs 11 weeks), and in patients with ECOG 0-1 treatment was a significant prognostic factor. In a retrospective review of 383 patients with advanced NSCLC receiving palliative chemotherapy, receiving fourth- or further-line therapy was independently associated with longer overall survival, with benefit concentrated in patients with good performance status (ECOG 0-1), while poor PS predicted poor outcome.

question: Can folic acid protect against congenital heart defects in Down syndrome?
answer: In a case-control analysis of liveborn children with Down syndrome, first-trimester folic acid use showed no protective effect against heart anomalies overall (adjusted OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.61-1.47). No protective effect was found for specific subtypes either, including conotruncal defects, ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defects, or endocardial cushion defects; exposure was similar in cases (49%) and controls (46%).

question: Is breast cancer prognosis inherited?
answer: A Swedish population-based cohort study found that breast cancer prognosis is familial: daughters and sisters of a proband with poor prognosis had a 60% higher 5-year breast cancer mortality than those of a proband with good prognosis (HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.2-2.2; p for trend 0.002). Five-year survival was lower among daughters whose mothers died within 5 years than among those whose mothers were alive (87% vs 91%, p=0.03), and the gap was larger among sisters (70% vs 88%, p=0.001). The association was slightly stronger among sisters (HR 1.8; 95% CI 1.0-3.4) than among daughters (HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.1-2.3).

question: Is laparoscopic adrenalectomy safe and effective for adrenal masses larger than 7 cm?
answer: In a retrospective series of 18 consecutive laparoscopic adrenalectomies for lesions larger than 7 cm (mean 8.3 cm), mean operative time was 137 min and mean blood loss 182 mL, with a 16% intraoperative complication rate and 3 conversions to open surgery, suggesting the procedure is feasible and reasonably safe. Most patients (15 of 18) were completed laparoscopically, indicating the approach can be effective for large adrenal masses in selected cases. Indirect evidence from a mixed laparoscopic adrenalectomy series shows pheochromocytomas, which were significantly larger than other tumors, had longer operating times, longer stays and most of the complications, yet no local recurrence was seen after laparoscopic resection.

question: Adults with mild intellectual disabilities: can their reading comprehension ability be improved?
answer: In a study of 38 adults with mild intellectual disability, a 15-week text comprehension strategy program (summarizing, questioning, clarifying, predicting) produced substantial gains on strategy tests and an even larger transfer effect on general text comprehension. question: Body diffusion-weighted MR imaging of uterine endometrial cancer: is it helpful in the detection of cancer in nonenhanced MR imaging?
answer: Adding diffusion-weighted (DW) imaging to nonenhanced T2-weighted MR imaging improved detection of endometrial cancer: sensitivity rose from 83% (19/23) with T2-weighted images alone to 96% when DW and fused DW/T2-weighted images were added, with 3 of the 4 previously missed cancers identified. The mean ADC value of endometrial cancer ((0.97±0.19)x10^-3 mm²/s) was significantly lower than that of normal endometrium, myometrium, leiomyoma and adenomyosis (p<0.05), which supports DW imaging as a way to distinguish cancer from these tissues.

The mean ADC value of endometrial cancer ((0.97±0.19)x10^-3 mm²/s) was significantly lower than that of normal endometrium, myometrium, leiomyoma and adenomyosis (p<0.05), which supports DW imaging as a way to distinguish cancer from these tissues.

question: Is severe macrosomia manifested at 11-14 weeks of gestation?
answer: Yes: in a case-control study, fetuses that became severely macrosomic were already larger than expected at 11-14 weeks, with a greater measured-minus-expected CRL difference than controls (6.66 mm vs 1.17 mm; 3 vs 0.5 days; both P<0.0001). The size discrepancy at NT screening correlated with the extent of macrosomia at birth (r = 0.47 for mm and r = 0.48 for days, both P<0.01).

question: Does somatostatin confer insulinostatic effects of neuromedin u in the rat pancreas?
answer: Somatostatin appears to mediate, at least in part, the insulinostatic effect of neuromedin U in the rat pancreas: NmU reduced insulin secretion from perfused rat pancreas and stimulated somatostatin secretion from isolated islets, and blocking somatostatin receptors with cyclosomatostatin reduced NmU-induced inhibition of insulin secretion. NmU stimulated somatostatin secretion at both physiological and supraphysiological glucose concentrations, and the NmUR1 receptor subtype (not NmUR2) was expressed in the endocrine pancreas, predominantly at the islet periphery.

question: Treadmill training post stroke: are there any secondary benefits?
answer: In a small matched-pair study of chronic stroke survivors, 12 sessions of treadmill walking were followed by significant within-group improvements in depression, mobility and social participation, but there was no significant difference between the treadmill and control groups on any measure. The control group, who received weekly phone calls, showed no significant change over time on these measures, whereas the treadmill group improved significantly on depression (P = 0.005, P<0.001), mobility (P = 0.008) and social participation (P = 0.004).

question: Sternal plating for primary and secondary sternal closure; can it improve sternal stability?
answer: In a human cadaver model, adding a transverse sternal plate to wire or cable closure raised the intrathoracic pressure needed to cause 2.0 mm sternal separation from about 183 to about 301, and closure with four plates alone raised it to about 355 (p<0.05), indicating improved sternal stability. Regression coefficients for the plate groups were 120 (95% CI 47-194) for wires/cables plus one plate and 142 (95% CI 66-219) for four plates alone, so plate fixation was associated with higher displacement pressures. In a separate cadaveric simulation, plated sternums withstood simulated chest compressions with no hardware failure or obvious visceral trauma, and rib fracture incidence was comparable to control.

question: Can magnetic resonance imaging accurately predict concordant pain provocation during provocative disc injection?
answer: Only a specific combined MR finding, disc protrusion with a high intensity zone (HIZ), predicted concordant pain on discography well (sensitivity 45.5%, specificity 97.8%, PPV 87.0%). Individual MR findings did not identify painful discs reliably. Disc degeneration (sensitivity 95.4%, specificity 38.8%, PPV 33.9%), disc protrusion alone (sensitivity 68.2%, specificity 80.6%, PPV 53.6%), and HIZ alone (sensitivity 56.8%, specificity 83.6%, PPV 53.2%) were not helpful in identifying a disc with concordant pain. A normal or bulging disc with HIZ was not associated with pain reproduction.

question: Treadmill testing of children who have spina bifida and are ambulatory: does peak oxygen uptake reflect maximum oxygen uptake?
answer: In 20 ambulatory children with spina bifida, treadmill VO2peak appeared to reflect true VO2max: there was no significant difference between VO2peak and VO2 during a supramaximal protocol, and 15 of 20 children met at least 2 of 3 established maximal-effort criteria. question: Standardizing care in medical oncology: are Web-based systems the answer?
answer: In an interview and observation study at 6 Australian hospitals, a Web-based oncology protocol system played a major role in guiding oncology treatment across participating sites, but its use varied by hospital location, clinician role and experience. Uptake depended on clinician factors (need for autonomy, perceived lack of time) and environmental factors (hospital policy on protocol use, endorsement of the system, sufficient computers and infrastructure). The education clinicians received about the system was integral to its ongoing use.

question: Is it necessary to insert a nasobiliary drainage tube routinely after endoscopic clearance of the common bile duct in patients with choledocholithiasis-induced cholangitis?
answer: Routine ENBD insertion after endoscopic clearance of CBD stones in acute cholangitis does not appear necessary. In a randomized trial of 104 patients, cholangitis recurrence at 24 weeks (3.9% vs 3.8%) and length of hospital stay (7.9 vs 7.9 days) did not differ between the ENBD and no-ENBD groups. ENBD placement added burden: procedure time was longer (26.2 vs 22.7 minutes) and patient discomfort scores were higher (4.9 vs 2.8) than without ENBD.

question: Diagnostic and therapeutic ureteroscopy: is dilatation of ureteral meatus always necessary?
answer: Dilatation of the ureteral meatus is not always necessary: in a retrospective comparison of 286 semirigid ureteroscopies, procedures done without meatal dilatation (95) had no statistically significant difference in peroperative or postoperative complications versus those done with dilatation (191), with an overall success rate of 86.5%. In a prospective series of 110 patients with lower ureteral stones, ureteroscopy achieved complete clearance without fluoroscopy in most patients, and balloon dilatation of the meatus was performed whenever required in 13 patients. In a randomized study of 60 patients comparing stented versus nonstented groups, ureteroscopic lithotripsy was performed with a 6Fr rigid ureteroscope without ureteral dilation, and the stone-free rate was 100% in each group.

question: Are patients willing participants in the new wave of community-based medical education in regional and rural Australia?
answer: Yes: in a survey of rural and regional New South Wales general practices, 118 of 122 patients (about 97%) consented to medical student involvement in their consultation, and patients were overwhelmingly positive about their doctor and practice being involved in student teaching. Before the consultation they were reluctant to let students conduct some or all aspects of it independently, but afterward they reported they would have accepted higher levels of involvement than actually occurred.

question: Does perspective-taking increase patient satisfaction in medical encounters?
answer: Across three randomized studies of 608 students, those given a perspective-taking instruction before a clinical skills exam earned higher standardized patient satisfaction scores than controls (Study 1 P = .01, effect size 0.16; Study 2 P = .001, 0.31; Study 3 P = .009, 0.13). The benefit extended to African American standardized patients, whose satisfaction improved with perspective-taking. The effect depended on baseline tendency: students with high baseline perspective-taking tendencies outscored controls (P = .0004, effect size 0.25), while those with low tendencies did not (P = .72, effect size 0.00).

question: Are adult body circumferences associated with height?
answer: In NHANES III adults, waist and hip circumferences were significantly associated with height after adjustment for age and race, scaling with powers of about 0.76 (waist) and 0.45 (hip) in men and 0.80 and 0.53 in women, equal to roughly 0.2 to 0.5 cm per cm of height. Univariate circumference-height models were weak or nonsignificant, and the association appeared only after adjusting for age and race. WC/height and HC/height ratios decreased as height increased in both sexes, and WC/HC decreased with height in women only. Other studies found height related to circumference in particular contexts: in Glasgow, residents of the most deprived neighbourhood were shorter and had larger waist circumferences, and in Manchester lower height and greater waist girth were independently related to plasma glucose.

question: Does minimal access major surgery in the newborn hurt less?
answer: In a retrospective matched cohort of neonates undergoing thoracoscopic repair of esophageal atresia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia, cumulative postoperative opioid doses did not differ significantly from conventional surgery at 12 h, 24 h, 48 h or 7 days, so minimal access surgery did not reduce opioid use. Postoperative pain scores were likewise similar between minimal access and conventional surgery groups in these neonates.

question: Are patients with serious mental illness more likely to be admitted to nursing homes with more deficiencies in care?
answer: In a national cohort of over 1.3 million new nursing home admissions in 2007, patients with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder tended to be admitted to nursing homes with more deficiencies than other patients. Patients with schizophrenia entered facilities with more total deficiencies (13.3 vs. 11.2) and more healthcare-related deficiencies (8.6 vs. 7.2) than other patients, all P<0.001. Patients with bipolar disorder also entered facilities with more total deficiencies (12.5 vs. 11.2) and more healthcare-related deficiencies (8.2 vs. 7.2), all P<0.001. The association between serious mental illness and admission to higher-deficiency nursing homes persisted after sequentially controlling for within-county facility choice, patient characteristics, and facility covariates.

question: Is endometrial polyp formation associated with increased expression of vascular endothelial growth factor and transforming growth factor-beta1?
answer: In a prospective study of 70 premenopausal women, endometrial polyps showed higher VEGF and TGF-β1 expression than adjacent endometrium, so polyp formation is associated with increased expression of both. VEGF scores in glandular cells were significantly higher in polyps than in adjacent endometrium in both the proliferative (P<0.001) and secretory (P=0.03) phases. Stromal VEGF was higher only in the proliferative phase (P=0.006). TGF-β1 in glandular cells was significantly higher in polyps only in the proliferative phase (P=0.02). Stromal TGF-β1 was higher in both the proliferative (P=0.006) and secretory (P=0.008) phases. VEGF and TGF-β1 expression correlated significantly with steroid receptor expression (estrogen and progesterone receptors).

question: MiraLAX vs. Golytely: is there a significant difference in the adenoma detection rate?
answer: In a post hoc analysis of an RCT of average-risk screening colonoscopy, Golytely was independently associated with higher adenoma detection than MiraLAX on multivariate analysis (2.28 times more likely, 95% CI 1.05-4.98, P=0.04). question: Does a colonoscopy after acute diverticulitis affect its management?
answer: In a retrospective review of 220 patients hospitalized for acute diverticulitis, early (4-6 week) colonoscopy in 100 patients found no colonic malignancy and led to no new or different diagnosis, suggesting it did not change management. Colonoscopy did find at least one polyp in 32% of patients, but only one was an advanced adenoma, and survival did not differ between patients with and without colonoscopy. A separate CT-based study found colon cancer in 2.2% of 402 patients who had colonoscopy after diverticulitis, with higher odds of cancer when CT showed lymph nodes, abscess, or obstruction with a localized mass, so colonoscopy may be informative in selected patients.

question: Does route of delivery affect maternal and perinatal outcome in women with eclampsia?
answer: In a randomized trial of 200 eclampsia cases at ≥34 weeks, route of delivery (cesarean vs vaginal) did not significantly change composite maternal outcomes (10.89% vs 7.07%; RR 1.54, 95% CI 0.62-3.81). Neonatal composite event rates were numerically lower with cesarean delivery (9.90% vs 19.19%; RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.25-1.05), but the difference was not statistically significant.

question: Can third trimester ultrasound predict the presentation of the first twin at delivery?
answer: Yes. In a retrospective cohort of 238 twin pregnancies, ultrasound-determined cephalic presentation of twin A had a positive predictive value of 95% for cephalic presentation at delivery after 28 weeks' gestation. question: Does cognitive function predict frequency compressed speech recognition in listeners with normal hearing and normal cognition?
answer: In 15 young normally-hearing adults with normal cognition, cognitive ability was significantly related to speech recognition in the unprocessed condition but not in the frequency-compressed conditions (2:1 and 3:1), so cognition did not predict frequency compressed speech recognition. question: Can early second-look tympanoplasty reduce the rate of conversion to modified radical mastoidectomy?
answer: In a single-surgeon series of 132 second-look operations after primary canal-wall-up (CAT) surgery, only 4 cases (3%) were converted to a modified radical mastoidectomy, and 3 cases needed a third-look procedure. question: Contrast-enhanced MR imaging of hand and finger joints in patients with early rheumatoid arthritis: do we really need a full dose of gadobenate dimeglumine for assessing synovial enhancement at 3 T?
answer: A full dose of gadobenate dimeglumine does not appear necessary at 3 T in early RA: half-dose (0.05 mmol/kg) and full-dose (0.1 mmol/kg) images showed no difference in RAMRIS, tenosynovitis scores, image quality, or assessment of synovial enhancement (P = 1). Half-dose imaging did give significantly lower synovial signal intensity than full dose (mean 914.35 vs 1022, P<.001), but the two were highly correlated (r = 0.875). A regression formula can convert normalized half-dose values to full-dose equivalents.

question: Globulomaxillary cysts--do they really exist?
answer: In a retrospective analysis of 17 cases primarily diagnosed as globulomaxillary cysts, the lesions were assigned to other entities: seven lateral periodontal cysts, four radicular cysts, two keratocystic odontogenic tumours, one adenomatoid odontogenic tumour, one periapical granuloma, one residual cyst and one undefined jaw cyst. The most frequent reassigned diagnosis was lateral periodontal cyst (7 of 17), followed by radicular cyst (4 of 17).

question: Can mental imagery functional magnetic resonance imaging predict recovery in patients with disorders of consciousness?
answer: In a small observational study of 22 patients with disorders of consciousness, activation on a mental imagery fMRI task predicted later recovery on the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised, especially in vegetative-state patients. All 5 vegetative-state patients with significant activation reached at least a minimally conscious state, while none of the 5 without activation did (sensitivity 100%, specificity 100%). In minimally conscious patients, prediction of emergence was less precise: 6 of 9 with activation emerged, but 1 of 3 without activation also emerged (sensitivity 85%, specificity 40%).

question: Telemedicine and type 1 diabetes: is technology per se sufficient to improve glycaemic control?
answer: In a 6-month study of patients using a smartphone insulin dose advisor, HbA1c improved in both high users (8.7% to 8.2%) and low users (9.0% to 8.5%). Among high users, adding telemonitoring/teleconsultation gave no extra HbA1c benefit (-0.49% vs -0.52%, P=0.879). Among low users, those who also received teleconsultation support tended to improve HbA1c more than those without it (-0.93% vs -0.46%, P=0.084). This suggests human support might matter where engagement with the technology is low, but the difference was not statistically significant. The proportion of meals using the insulin dose advisor stayed stable in high users but fell in low users (36.6% to 26.7%, P=0.005).

question: Steroids in aminoglycoside-containing ear drops: do they reduce cochlear toxicity?
answer: In a controlled mouse study, intratympanic gentamicin alone caused significant hearing loss versus untreated ears (6.59 dB, P = .010). Gentamicin combined with betamethasone (with benzalkonium chloride) did not cause significant hearing loss versus untreated ears (3.56 dB, P = .242), which points toward reduced cochlear toxicity with the steroid. Betamethasone alone was associated with significantly greater hearing loss than untreated ears (6.48 dB, P = .007), so the apparent protective effect arose even though the steroid alone was not benign in this model.

question: Does sex influence the response to intravenous thrombolysis in ischemic stroke?
answer: In a very large registry of 45,079 alteplase-treated patients, there was no sex difference in 3-month functional independence after adjustment (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.09), so sex did not meaningfully alter functional response to thrombolysis. In the same registry, adjusted analysis showed male sex was associated with higher mortality (OR 1.19) and higher symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage risk (OR 1.25), indicating some small sex-related differences in safety outcomes. In 369 rt-PA-treated patients with transcranial Doppler monitoring, men and women had similar recanalization rates (complete recanalization 34.2% vs 31.2%, p=0.6), and regression showed no sex difference in recanalization, time to recanalization, or 3-month clinical outcome.

question: Is digoxin use for cardiovascular disease associated with risk of prostate cancer?
answer: In a population-based case-control study (1,001 cases, 942 controls), digoxin use was associated with lower odds of prostate cancer after adjustment, but the result was not statistically significant (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.30-1.10). Among men with 3 or more PSA tests in the preceding 5 years (546 cases, 380 controls), the inverse association was stronger and statistically significant (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.20-0.98).

question: Is the determination of specific IgE against components using ISAC 112 a reproducible technique?
answer: Specific IgE determination with ImmunoCAP ISAC 112 showed good reproducibility: intra- and inter-assay agreement was very good for 94 allergens and good for one, and the mean CV was 9.4% for the calibrator and 22.9% for patient sera. Reproducibility was somewhat lower across batches and laboratories. Inter-batch agreement was very good for 82 allergens, good for 14, moderate for 5, poor for one and bad for one. Inter-laboratory agreement was very good for 73, good for 22, moderate for 6 and poor for 2.

question: HIF1A as a major vascular endothelial growth factor regulator: do its polymorphisms have an association with age-related macular degeneration?
answer: In a study of 87 AMD patients and 80 controls, the HIF1A polymorphisms rs11549465 and rs11549467 showed no statistically significant difference in distribution between patients and healthy subjects, so no association with AMD was found. question: Does radiotherapy of the primary rectal cancer affect prognosis after pelvic exenteration for recurrent rectal cancer?
answer: In a retrospective review of 87 patients undergoing pelvic exenteration for locally recurrent rectal cancer, prior radiotherapy for the primary tumour was associated with worse outcomes, including lower disease-free survival (p = 0.022). Patients previously irradiated for the primary cancer needed more radical exenterations (68% vs 44%), had lower rates of clear resection margins (63% vs 87%), and had more surgical complications per patient. Among patients with clear margins, overall survival and disease-free survival were still lower in the previously irradiated group, and the survival difference persisted after adjusting for T and N stage of the primary tumour.

question: Rectal cancer threatening or affecting the prostatic plane: is partial prostatectomy oncologically adequate?
answer: In a retrospective multicentre series of 126 men with rectal cancer threatening or affecting the prostatic plane, partial prostatectomy after preoperative chemoradiotherapy gave a free anterior circumferential resection margin in all cases, and the overall CRM-positive rate after chemoradiotherapy plus prostatic resection was 2.4%. Without preoperative chemoradiotherapy, CRM positivity was much higher: 25.0% when the anterior margin was threatened and 41.7% when it was affected. With preoperative radiotherapy the rates were 7.1% and 20.7%, respectively. Oncological adequacy came with a morbidity cost: intra-operative urethral damage occurred in 36.4% of patients undergoing partial prostatectomy, and a postoperative urinary fistula developed in 18.2%.

question: Literacy after cerebral hemispherectomy: Can the isolated right hemisphere read?
answer: In seven individuals with left hemispherectomy for perinatal-infarct epilepsy, about 60% developed average-range word and paragraph reading, indicating the isolated right hemisphere can support reading. question: Preparing patients at high risk of falls for discharge home after rehabilitation: Do we meet the guidelines?
answer: In a retrospective audit of 50 high-falls-risk patients discharged home after inpatient rehabilitation, practice fell short of guideline expectations: discharge documentation correctly identified falls risk for only nine of the 50 patients. Assessment of several risk factors was rarely documented, including osteoporosis (n=8), footwear (n=4) and visual assessment in the previous 2 years (n=1). Patients had a median of 8 of 17 risk factors and received a median of 6.5 of 16 possible prevention strategies. Mobility (n=48), strength (n=44) and personal activities of daily living training (n=43) were the most common strategies. Where a risk factor was present, a corresponding strategy was documented in more than 80% of records for 12 of the risk factors, so some aspects of preparation were well covered.

answer: In a prospective whole-body MRI study of 86 patients with bone metastases, T1w detected significantly more metastases than STIR at both 1.5 T and 3 T (sensitivity 99.72–100% for T1w vs 70.99–79.34% for STIR). question: Does cup-cage reconstruction with oversized cups provide initial stability in THA for osteoporotic acetabular fractures?
answer: In a prospective radiostereometric study of 10 patients older than 70 with acute acetabular fractures treated by immediate THA with an oversized cup and cup-cage, median 1-year proximal migration was 0.83 mm and sagittal rotation 1.3°, within primary-THA limits for most patients. Seven of the 10 components stayed within the migration limits that predict later loosening in primary THA (1.76 mm proximal, 2.53° sagittal rotation), while three exceeded them at 1 year. The contact surface between the cup and the unfractured pelvis was small, ranging from 11 to 17 cm² (15%-27% of each component), yet the reconstructions were mobilized without weightbearing restrictions.

question: Utility of unenhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MRI in children with sickle cell disease -- can it differentiate bone infarcts from acute osteomyelitis?
answer: In a retrospective study of 31 children with sickle cell disease and acute bone pain, bone marrow signal intensity on unenhanced T1-weighted fat-saturated MRI did not significantly differentiate bone infarct from acute osteomyelitis (P = 0.56). question: Are financial incentives cost-effective to support smoking cessation during pregnancy?
answer: In a cost-effectiveness analysis based on a Phase II RCT of 612 pregnant women in Glasgow, financial incentives of up to £400 had an incremental cost of £1127 per cotinine-validated quitter at 34-38 weeks, and a lifetime model gave an ICER of £482 per QALY from the NHS perspective. The cost per quitter was similar to a standard look-up value from published ICER tables (£1390 per quitter), and the lifetime model showed an incremental cost of only £17 with a gain of 0.04 QALYs.

question: Do Wound Cultures Give Information About the Microbiology of Blood Cultures in Severe Burn Patients?
answer: In a retrospective study of 195 severe burn patients, wound cultures carried information about blood culture pathogens: 44% of blood isolates had previously been documented in wound cultures, and the same pathogen was transmitted from wound to blood in 65% of bacteremic patients. Across all severe burn patients in the cohort (88 of whom had at least one bloodstream infection episode), same-pathogen wound-to-blood transmission was documented in 30%, and BSI frequency rose as the Ryan score increased.

question: Treatment of contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion: Is less more?
answer: Managing a contralateral hydrocele in neonatal testicular torsion solely through a scrotal approach (opened at the time of contralateral scrotal fixation, without inguinal exploration) appeared safe and effective: none of the patients with a hydrocele developed a clinical hydrocele or hernia after an average 7.5 years of follow-up. question: Could chest wall rigidity be a factor in rapid death from illicit fentanyl abuse?
answer: Post-mortem data from 48 fentanyl deaths suggest chest wall rigidity could be a factor in rapid death: no measurable norfentanyl was found in 42% of cases and levels were under 1 ng/ml in another 52%, which the authors read as very rapid death consistent with acute chest rigidity. Some deaths had very high fentanyl concentrations (e.g., 22 and 20 ng/ml) with no norfentanyl detected, and elevated fentanyl did not track with norfentanyl levels, which fits a rapid-onset mechanism after intravenous use. Deaths also occurred at low, therapeutic-range fentanyl levels (1-2 ng/ml) in apparent non-naïve opioid users, and the authors note that rapid IV fentanyl can produce chest wall rigidity, which they say is unknown within the drug abuse community.

question: The Prevalence of Incidentally Detected Idiopathic Misty Mesentery on Multidetector Computed Tomography: Can Obesity Be the Triggering Cause?

question: Does Viral Co-Infection Influence the Severity of Acute Respiratory Infection in Children?
answer: In a prospective Spanish multicenter cohort of 204 children admitted with acute respiratory infection, the number of detected viruses did not correlate with any marker of severity. Bacterial superinfection, rather than viral co-infection, was associated with greater severity: higher odds of PICU admission, respiratory support, higher clinical score and longer hospital stay. Pneumococcal vaccination was associated with lower severity markers, and all findings were replicated in an independent UK cohort of 97 children.

question: Do risk calculators accurately predict surgical site occurrences?
answer: Existing risk calculators did not predict surgical site occurrences (SSO) accurately after open ventral hernia repair: in a multicenter retrospective database (n=795), AUCs for SSO were low (0.52–0.60). In a small single-center prospective cohort (n=88), SSO AUCs were also low (0.50–0.69), with the best (ACS-NSQIP, 0.69) still only modest. Several models did stratify patients into tiers with significantly different SSO rates (VHRS and HW-RAT in the multicenter set; ACS-NSQIP in the prospective set). Calibration was poor: VHRS, VHWG and CDC wound class overestimated SSO and SSI risk, while HW-RAT and ACS-NSQIP underestimated risk in all groups.

question: Does the treatment of amblyopia normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in amblyopic children?
answer: Six months of amblyopia treatment (full refractive correction, adaptation, and patching) did not normalise subfoveal choroidal thickness in anisometropic hyperopic amblyopic children: there was no significant pre- versus post-treatment change in the amblyopic eyes (p = 0.428). Choroidal thickness remained significantly greater in amblyopic eyes than in fellow eyes after treatment (p = 0.006), even though visual acuity in the amblyopic eyes improved significantly from 0.35 to 0.16 logMAR (p < 0.001). Fellow eyes also showed no significant change in choroidal thickness after treatment (p = 0.343), and the initial choroidal thickness was significantly higher in amblyopic eyes than in fellow eyes (p = 0.019).

question: Prostate bed target interfractional motion using RTOG consensus definitions and daily CT on rails : Does target motion differ between superior and inferior portions of the clinical target volume?
answer: In eight postprostatectomy patients (300 fractions) imaged with daily CT-on-rails, no statistically significant difference in interfractional motion was found between the superior (SUP-CTV) and inferior (INF-CTV) prostate bed CTV in any direction (LR, SI, AP). Mean target motion (bone to RTOG-defined area) was small and similar in both portions: INF-CTV 0.1, 0.5 and 0.2 mm versus SUP-CTV 0.3, 0.5 and 0 mm in LR, SI and AP directions, respectively. Variability in the AP direction was numerically larger for SUP-CTV (SD 5.0 mm) than INF-CTV (SD 2.5 mm), though this was not a statistically significant difference in motion.

Mean target motion (bone to RTOG-defined area) was small and similar in both portions: INF-CTV 0.1, 0.5 and 0.2 mm versus SUP-CTV 0.3, 0.5 and 0 mm in LR, SI and AP directions, respectively.

question: Do prerecorded lecture VODcasts affect lecture attendance of first-yearpre-clinical Graduate Entry to Medicine students?
answer: In surveys of first-year Graduate Entry to Medicine students given prerecorded Physiology VODcasts before live lectures, attendance stayed high: 84.3% attended all 21 lectures and only 4% missed more than one lecture in each series. This suggests VODcast availability did not reduce live lecture attendance. Most students (79%) said VODcasts should not replace live lectures, which is consistent with continued valuing of live attendance.

question: Are serum leptin levels a prognostic factor in advanced lung cancer?
answer: In one study of 71 previously untreated lung cancer patients, serum leptin levels showed no association with overall survival, so leptin was not found to be a prognostic factor. In the same study, leptin did not differ by ECOG performance status, weight loss, histological type, disease stage or TNM classification. Leptin was lower in patients than in matched controls (4.75±4.91 vs 9.67±8.02 ng/ml) and correlated with BMI.

limitations.text: The only study that directly tested leptin against survival was small (71 patients), single-center and had no replication. It reported no multivariable survival analysis, and the stated BMI correlation p-value (p>0.010) appears inconsistent.

The other leptin study in lung cancer was a case-control study of NSCLC risk, not survival. It cannot show whether leptin predicts prognosis, and it points the other way on diagnostic association (elevated leptin as a risk factor), which conflicts with the lower leptin seen in cases elsewhere.
